options: Which untracked files Git should never stage automatically
Which files are deleted from disk
Which commits get pushed to a remote
Which branches can be merged
questions.explain: .gitignore lists patterns for untracked files Git should leave alone — it never touches files already being tracked.

questions.q: What happens if you add an already-committed file's pattern to .gitignore?
options: Nothing — .gitignore only affects files Git doesn't already track
The file is immediately deleted from the repository's history
The file is automatically untracked
Git throws an error
questions.explain: .gitignore has no retroactive effect on already-tracked files; you must explicitly untrack them with git rm --cached.

questions.q: Which of these is a real example this lesson gives of something data projects accidentally commit?
options: A .env file with a database password, or a 400MB CSV export
A README.md file
A .gitignore file itself
A commit message
questions.explain: Credentials in .env files and large raw data exports are common accidental commits that .gitignore is meant to prevent.

options: Stops tracking the file in Git without deleting it from the working directory
Permanently deletes the file from disk
Reverts the file to its last committed version
Renames the file
questions.explain: --cached removes a file from Git's tracking while leaving the actual file on disk untouched.

questions.q: If real credentials were accidentally committed, is untracking the file with git rm --cached enough to fully fix it?
options: No — the credential is still recoverable from the repository's history, so it must be rotated
Yes — untracking permanently erases it from history
Yes, but only if you also delete the .gitignore file
No — you must delete the entire repository
questions.explain: Untracking stops future tracking, but the credential remains in earlier commits' history, so it must be rotated to be truly safe.
